stem: Drag the legs to make a right-angled triangle in which $\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$. Any size of triangle that works is correct: it is the ratio that has to match.
solution: $\sin\theta = \dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$, so for $\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$ take the opposite side as 1 and the hypotenuse as $\sqrt{5}$.
The hypotenuse follows from the two legs, so find the adjacent leg with the Theorem of Pythagoras: $\text{adjacent}^2 = (\sqrt{5})^2 - 1^2 = 4$, so the adjacent side is 2.
Drag the legs to 1 (the side opposite $\theta$) and 2 (the side adjacent to $\theta$). The hypotenuse is $\sqrt{1^2+2^2} = \sqrt{5}$, so $\sin\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$, already in surd form.
Any triangle whose legs are in the ratio 1 : 2 gives the same value. Legs 2 and 4 have hypotenuse $\sqrt{2^2+4^2} = 2\sqrt{5}$, and $\sin\theta = \dfrac{2}{2\sqrt{5}} = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$.

With the two legs swapped (opposite 2, adjacent 1) the same triangle gives $\sin\theta = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{5}}$ and $\cos\theta = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}$. The sine of one acute angle is the cosine of the other, so check which leg faces $\theta$.
notes: Exercises the same skill as the book's surd-triangle questions (Pythagoras gives a surd hypotenuse, the ratio is written in surd form, size is irrelevant) but run backwards, from a surd ratio to whole-number legs. The book's own triangles cannot be built here: 6, 6sqrt(3), 12 and 9, 3sqrt(3), 6sqrt(3) need legs in the ratio 1:sqrt(3), which no lattice drag reaches, so this uses a non-special 1-2-sqrt(5) triangle (see the gap for this objective). 1/sqrt(5) was chosen because no other whole-number leg pair up to 12 has a sine within 0.03 of it, so no accidental near-match is accepted. Own=false ids are the prerequisite misconceptions listed under this objective. used-cosine (legs swapped, so the triangle is the other angle's) is the likeliest error and is listed first. used-tangent fires only when the tangent readout happens to land within the grader's tolerance of 0.4472 (it is irrational, so only an approximate lattice match such as legs 4 and 9 can); if the tolerance is tight it rarely fires. off-target is not mapped: a forgotten Pythagoras (hypotenuse taken as 5 rather than sqrt(5)) and a plain guess land there equally, so neither dominates.
